Republicans Criticize Trump's Media Ban as Self-Defeating Ahead of Midterms
item.description: President Donald Trump's decision to ban three major media outlets—MS NOW, CNN, and Politico—from the White House has drawn sharp criticism from within his own party. The move, announced on Friday and implemented Saturday, was met with a collective sigh from prominent Republicans, who argue it is poorly timed and counterproductive. Trump accused the outlets of reporting 'FICTION and LIES' and warned that other 'Fake News Media Outlets' would face similar bans in the future. The White House's action has sparked mounting accusations of First Amendment violations, as the administration faces growing scrutiny over its approach to media relations. Douglas Heye, former communications director for the Republican National Committee, told The New York Times that Trump's 'brash tactics' are unhelpful, especially with the midterms just weeks away. He emphasized that the focus should be on Trump's economic plans, not media disputes. Sarah Matthews, a lifelong conservative and former deputy press s

item.title: New York City Reports More West Nile Virus Cases in 2026 Than Full Year of 2025
item.description: New York City has reported 23 confirmed cases of West Nile Virus (WNV) in 2026, surpassing the total of 18 cases recorded throughout all of 2025. According to the city's health department, these cases are distributed across all five boroughs, with the highest numbers in Brooklyn (7 cases), followed by the Bronx (3), Queens (3), Staten Island (3), Manhattan (2). The data shows a significant increase compared to previous years, with 46 cases in 2022, 32 in 2023, and 36 in 2024. Health officials note that most people infected with WNV do not develop symptoms, but approximately one in 150 develop severe neuroinvasive disease, which can cause neurological symptoms, muscle weakness, and brain swelling. Of the 23 confirmed cases in 2026, 18 were classified as West Nile neuroinvasive disease, while five were categorized as West Nile fever with no central nervous system involvement. item.title: Top VPN Services of 2026: Comprehensive Review of Privacy and Performance
item.description: In this comprehensive review, WIRED tested and evaluated the top VPN services available in 2026, focusing on privacy, security, and performance. The article highlights Private Internet Access (PIA) as a long-standing provider with a strong privacy record, noting that PIA successfully defended its no-logging policy during a criminal investigation in 2016. However, PIA's performance was poor, with speed drops exceeding 50% on the closest US server. MysteriumVPN, a decentralized VPN (dVPN), was criticized for its slow speeds and lack of transparency, including no third-party audits or privacy materials. PrivadoVPN offers a free tier with limited data (10GB/month) but lacks transparency reports and audits, making it less appealing compared to competitors like Proton and Windscribe. The article also warns against several free VPNs, including Hola, which uses a peer-to-peer network and logs user data, and X-VPN, which has inconsistent protocols and potential ties to Chinese government entiti

item.title: RFK Jr. tells anti-vaccine group he will pursue vaccine safety questions as Health Secretary
item.description:
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. addressed a convention of Children's Health Defense, the anti-vaccine organization he founded, and told attendees they have 'a strong and steadfast friend at the White House.' Kennedy said he would 'die with my boots on' pursuing answers about vaccine risks, signaling a notable shift from earlier this year when White House advisers had urged him to avoid the vaccine issue given broad public support for childhood immunizations.
His remarks came one day after Dr. Nicole Saphier, President Trump's nominee for surgeon general, defended vaccine safety and efficacy during her Senate confirmation hearing. Kennedy began his speech by discussing food safety and nutrition, topics with wider political appeal, before turning to vaccines in a conference marked by misinformation and references to discredited studies.

item.title: UN General Assembly Condemns U.S. Visa Sanctions Against Palestinian Leader
item.description: The United Nations General Assembly has rebuked the Trump administration for blocking Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas from attending the annual UN General Assembly meeting in New York. The U.S. government extended visa sanctions against Palestinian officials, including Abbas, accusing them of working to 'internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.' In a near-unanimous vote of 152-3, the UN members voted to allow Abbas to participate virtually in the upcoming meeting. The resolution was supported by the majority of UN members, who condemned the U.S. for barring a head of state from attending the event. Chinese U.N. Deputy Permanent Representative Sun Lei stated that the United Nations Headquarters Agreement requires the host country to issue visas to representatives of Member States participating in UN meetings. She emphasized that depriving Palestine of the right to present its case before the UN is 'without legal basis, unacceptable in conscience, and indefensible in reason

item.title: California Enacts New Election Protection Laws Ahead of Midterms
item.description:
California Governor Gavin Newsom has signed a package of 13 new bills designed to protect the state's midterm elections from potential interference by the Trump administration. The legislation, developed in collaboration with Democratic lawmakers, aims to counter possible federal efforts to disrupt California's voting processes, particularly its extensive use of mail-in ballots, which President Trump has repeatedly criticized despite using absentee voting himself.
Key provisions include a ban on the seizure of ballots, election documents, or voting equipment before official election certification. Another measure makes it a felony for officials to order employees to interfere with the delivery or return of mail ballots. The legislation also prohibits arrests within 200 feet of polling places on Election Day, except in cases of election disruption or crimes against people or property, addressing concerns that federal agents might be deployed to polling sites in immigrant communities.

item.title: Brian Stelter Explains How Trump's White House Press Ban Could Reduce Presidential Media Coverage
item.description: CNN's Brian Stelter provided a detailed analysis of the potential consequences of President Donald Trump's recent decision to ban certain news outlets from the White House press pool. Stelter, a prominent CNN journalist, explained that the White House's exclusion of CNN, MS Now, and Politico from the press pool would create practical challenges for the administration. He noted that the five major TV networks that rotate coverage of the president - CNN, ABC, NBC, Fox News, and MS Now - have established infrastructure and resources to provide 24/7 coverage. By banning CNN and MS Now, the White House is creating a situation where there may be no media coverage available for the president during his public appearances on certain days. Stelter emphasized that Trump 'deeply cares about' being on camera regularly, but the press ban could significantly reduce his media exposure. He stated, 'Trump wants attention but not accountability. He wants the cameras and, in some cases, the photos, but h

item.title: io_uring Maintainer Proposes Thread Identity Handoff to Improve Asynchronous I/O Performance
item.description: The io_uring subsystem in the Linux kernel, designed for asynchronous I/O operations, has faced challenges maintaining its 'never blocks' guarantee due to kernel paths not originally designed for asynchronous execution. Jens Axboe, the io_uring maintainer, has proposed an RFC patch set introducing a 'thread identity handoff' mechanism to address this issue. Currently, operations that might block are handed off to a separate worker thread, incurring context-switch costs even when blocking doesn't occur. Axboe's solution involves a scheduler modification where a new flag (PF_IO_HANDOFF) is added to task_struct. When a thread about to block has this flag set, the scheduler calls io_uring_task_sleeping(), allowing io_uring to exchange the identities of the submitting thread and a worker thread. The worker thread assumes the submitting thread's identity, continues processing, and returns to user space, while the original thread blocks and later resumes. This approach avoids unnecessary cont

item.title: Middle East conflict threatens GOP midterm hopes as oil prices rise amid Houthi attacks
item.description: The Republican Party's prospects for the upcoming midterm elections are facing a significant setback due to a new crisis unfolding in the Middle East, according to analysts. The situation involves the Houthi militant group, which has claimed responsibility for missile attacks on Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, and energy infrastructure along the Red Sea coast. These attacks, occurring just six weeks before the November elections, have the potential to further increase global oil prices, which have already been rising in recent days. CNN national security analyst Alex Plitsas warned that the attacks on Saudi oil facilities create a 'quite the predicament' for the United States, as Saudi Arabia is a major U.S. ally. Failing to respond to the attacks could damage the U.S.-Saudi alliance while also potentially creating a second choke point in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which could further disrupt oil shipments and drive prices higher. item.title: New Law Extends Educator Tax Deduction to Early Childhood Teachers
item.description:
A new federal law signed on September 18, 2026, extends the Educator Expense Deduction to preschool teachers and child care workers for the first time, allowing them to claim tax write-offs for out-of-pocket classroom supply purchases when filing their 2026 tax returns. The bipartisan legislation, known as the Supporting Early-Childhood Educators' Deductions (SEED) Act, was authored by Senator Susan Collins of Maine and Senator Michael Bennet of Colorado and amends the Internal Revenue Code to include early childhood education programs alongside K-12 schools.
Previously, only kindergarten through 12th grade teachers could deduct up to $350 in unreimbursed classroom expenses such as books, crayons, and other teaching materials. This exclusion created an inequity where preschool educators working in the same buildings as K-12 teachers could not access the same tax benefit despite facing similar out-of-pocket costs. item.title: Karl Rove's Trump Impression Draws Applause at The Atlantic Event
item.description: Veteran Republican strategist Karl Rove recently delivered a remarkably accurate impression of former President Donald Trump during an event hosted by The Atlantic, leaving attendees and online observers astonished. The incident occurred when Rove, former White House Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy under George W. Bush, mimicked Trump's voice and mannerisms while repeating the phrase 'stone cold loser'—a term Trump had used to describe Rove in a Truth Social post. Rove had previously angered Trump by publishing an op-ed criticizing the growing bigotry within the Republican Party and announcing his intention to vote for a Democratic candidate. During the event, Rove's performance included moving his hand and frowning in a manner reminiscent of Trump, which prompted laughter and enthusiastic applause from the audience. item.title: Conservative Analysts Identify Turning Point in Trump's Second-Term Agenda
item.description: The article discusses a guest essay published in The New York Times by Peter Wehner, a former Reagan administration official, and Jonathan Rauch, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution. They argue that President Donald Trump has already failed in his most ambitious project: remaking American society through a second-term agenda. The authors identify a pivotal moment when Trump's power began to decline, specifically referencing the administration's retreat from Minneapolis after peaceful resistance to Operation Metro Surge, an immigration crackdown. This event marked the beginning of a series of setbacks, including plummeting approval ratings, court challenges to initiatives, and the fracturing of the MAGA coalition. Wehner and Rauch note that Trump's grip on power has weakened, with the MAGA movement showing signs of disintegration and the president no longer inspiring the fear he once did. The essay emphasizes that American civil society proved more resilient than MAGA's cultura

item.title: Turkey Revokes Iran's Bank Mellat License Amid U.S. Sanctions Pressure
item.description: Turkey has revoked the license of Iran's Bank Mellat, a Tehran-based financial institution that has been subject to Western sanctions for years, citing threats to financial system stability. The decision, announced in the official gazette on Saturday, September 19, 2026, follows recent U.S. sanctions on a Turkish bank over alleged ties to Iran's Revolutionary Guards. The Turkish banking regulator cited Article 71b of the banking law, stating that Bank Mellat's continued operation poses a threat to depositors' rights and the security of the financial system. Bank Mellat, partly owned by the Iranian government, has been under sanctions since 2015, when the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) was signed to curb Iran's nuclear program. However, the U.S. withdrew from the deal in 2018, reimposing economic sanctions. The bank was also sanctioned in 2019 for allegedly supporting Iran's Revolutionary Guards. item.title: Nursing Home Bed Shortages Grow as Baby Boomers Age
item.description: Nursing homes across the United States are reducing their capacity at a time when demand for long-term care is expected to surge. Facilities operated by ArchCare, a nonprofit affiliated with the Archdiocese of New York, have cut 269 beds over the past year and a half, representing a decline of nearly 12 percent. Some locations have stopped admitting new patients entirely, while others have closed entire floors. This trend is not isolated to New York. Since 2020, 24 nursing homes have closed in New York State alone, eliminating more than 3,000 licensed beds. Nationwide, the number of nursing facilities has dropped by over 900 in the past decade, according to federal data. The timing of these closures is particularly concerning because the oldest baby boomers are turning 80 this year, an age when the need for skilled nursing and long-term care rises sharply. item.title: Researchers Reconstruct the Wind Field of the Great Miami Hurricane of 1926
item.description:
Researchers at the University of Miami have reconstructed the wind field of the Great Miami Hurricane of 1926, providing a more detailed picture of one of the most destructive storms in South Florida's history. The Category 4 hurricane struck just south of downtown Miami in the early morning of September 18, 1926, producing estimated winds of 145 mph and killing more than 100 people in the Miami area while leaving thousands homeless. The disaster also contributed to the collapse of Florida's 1920s land boom and affected the newly established University of Miami, although the university resumed operations and began classes in late October.
Tropical cyclone expert Brian McNoldy created six-hourly wind field maps covering the storm's approximately 11-day lifetime. Because many of the measurements available in 1926 were incomplete, the reconstruction combines historical observations with estimates of tropical-storm-force wind radii, eyewall size, storm motion, latitude, and other characte

item.title: Cold Muonium Beam Could Enable the First Gravity Test of a Second-Generation Particle
item.description:
Researchers at ETH Zurich and the Paul Scherrer Institute have developed a method for producing a controlled beam of muonium, an exotic atom that could enable a new test of Einstein’s equivalence principle. Muonium consists of a positively charged antimuon, the antimatter counterpart of the muon, bound to a negatively charged electron. Because the muon is a heavier relative of the electron and belongs to the second generation of fundamental particles, measuring muonium’s response to gravity would extend tests of universal free fall beyond ordinary, first-generation matter.
The experiment is challenging because muons survive for only about 2.2 microseconds before decaying. Previous methods also produced muonium atoms with a wide range of speeds and directions, making precise measurements difficult. item.title: White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles Allegedly Behind Leaks Contradicting Trump's Statements
item.description: According to a recent report by Michael Wolff, a biographer of Donald Trump, the White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles is the likely source behind recent leaks that contradict the president's public statements. Wolff made these remarks during a Saturday episode of 'Inside Trump's Head,' where he analyzed two significant stories published in the New York Times and The Washington Post on the same day. Both articles featured unnamed advisers within the White House who were pushing back against Trump's positions on key issues. The first story addressed Trump's dismissal of concerns about artificial intelligence (AI) as a 'hoax,' while the second warned him to be more concerned about the upcoming midterm elections. Wolff noted that the leaks were not typical, as they were described as coming from 'advisers' rather than a single 'adviser,' suggesting coordination among multiple high-level officials. item.title: Pete Davidson and Colin Jost Turn a Retired Staten Island Ferry Into a One-Night Comedy Venue
item.description:
Pete Davidson and Colin Jost hosted a one-night comedy event aboard a retired Staten Island Ferry, turning their long-discussed boat project into a temporary performance venue on Manhattan’s East River. More than 300 people who had registered online for free tickets arrived at Pier 17 near the South Street Seaport and boarded the vessel, which was temporarily renamed the “Snapple Island Ferry” after the sponsoring beverage company.
Davidson and Jost opened the evening with a brief, informal seven-minute performance before introducing a lineup of established and emerging New York City comedians. The event combined stand-up comedy with the novelty of being on a large, inactive ferry, although the experience was reportedly uncomfortable for some attendees because of the heat and motion of the boat. The title’s description of the debut as “hot and nauseous” reflects those conditions rather than a major controversy.

item.title: Sharon Stone Recalls Ex-Husband's Unauthorized Brain Surgery Consent After 2001 Stroke
item.description: Sharon Stone, the 68-year-old actress, has shared a harrowing account of a medical incident that occurred in 2001 following a subarachnoid hemorrhage and stroke. During a recent appearance on the 'Mayim Bialik's Breakdown' podcast, Stone recounted waking up on a gurney being wheeled to exploratory brain surgery without her consent. Her then-husband, Phil Bronstein, allegedly signed her up for the procedure while she was in the neurological intensive care unit, where she was experiencing fluctuating consciousness due to her medical condition. Stone described the moment she realized she had not consented to the surgery, stating, 'I woke up again because the gurney hit something on the floor.' She further detailed how she confronted the doctor who claimed to have spoken with People magazine about her surgery, saying, 'You can't do that. I'm on the phone with People magazine.' item.title: California Governor Newsom Signs Bills to Protect Electoral Process Amid Trump Midterm Concerns
item.description: California Governor Gavin Newsom has signed a package of 13 bills aimed at safeguarding the state's electoral process ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. The legislation, which includes measures to make it a felony to seize ballots and election records, and to prohibit deceptive political attack ads created using artificial intelligence, was signed on September 19, 2026. Newsom stated that the bills are designed to prevent disruptions to California's elections, particularly in response to fears that the Trump administration may interfere with the electoral process. The governor emphasized that 'California will stop him at every opportunity,' referring to President Donald Trump's efforts to exert control over voting systems. California Attorney General Rob Bonta supported the legislation, noting that it comes after a recent U.S. Supreme Court victory that blocked the Trump administration from implementing sweeping changes to mail voting for the November midterms. item.title: Iran Proposes Conditions to End Conflict with U.S. Amid Rising Tensions
item.description: The White House has reportedly received a new offer from Iran to end the ongoing conflict, according to a senior Iranian official speaking to Al Jazeera. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, stated that Tehran communicated its conditions for ending the war through Qatari mediators. The conditions include a halt to hostilities across the region, unfreezing of Iranian assets, and lifting the U.S. naval blockade on the Strait of Hormuz. Rezaei emphasized that a response from President Trump is awaited, and warned that if the conditions are not accepted, Iran is prepared for an extended conflict. He also criticized Trump's assessments of Iran, stating that the war was instigated by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and that Iran is well-prepared to counter U.S. military actions, including recent tests of an anti-ship missile near a U.S. aircraft carrier. item.title: Chinese Private Space Companies Start Deploying Megaconstellation Satellites
item.description: Chinese private space companies are beginning to launch satellites for megaconstellations, marking a significant step in the country's space industry development. The recent launches of Zhuque 2E Y7 and Yinli 1 Y3 represent the first commercial satellite deployments by Chinese private enterprises in this sector. These launches are part of a broader trend where private companies are increasingly taking on roles traditionally held by government agencies in space exploration and satellite deployment. The Zhuque 2E Y7 satellite, developed by a Chinese private company, is designed to provide global internet coverage, while the Yinli 1 Y3 satellite focuses on Earth observation and remote sensing applications. This development is significant as it demonstrates China's growing capability in the commercial space sector, which has been dominated by state-owned enterprises for decades. item.title: Farm-state Republicans oppose Trump's beef import plan ahead of Senate elections
item.description:
President Donald Trump's plan to import 300,000 metric tons of tariff-free foreign beef, sold at 25 percent below current market prices, has drawn sharp criticism from Republicans in key cattle-producing states including Nebraska, Texas, Kansas, and Iowa. These farm-state Republicans worry the policy will undercut domestic ranchers and harm an industry already struggling with high fuel and fertilizer costs.
The timing is politically sensitive, as all four states have competitive Senate races this cycle. Independent Senate candidate Dan Osborn in Nebraska has launched attack ads accusing politicians of 'selling out American farmers and ranchers,' while Democrats in Kansas and Iowa are using the issue to appeal to rural voters who have traditionally supported Republicans.
Republican officials are caught between supporting Trump's goal of lowering beef prices for consumers and protecting ranchers who fear the import plan will depress cattle futures and damage their livelihoods. Senate A

item.title: Man with Self-Embedded Foreign Objects Undergoes Surgery After Medical Discovery
item.description: A 35-year-old man in China presented to a hospital with symptoms of discomfort during urination and blood in his urine. Initial examinations revealed stable vital signs and no obvious distress, but imaging tests detected unusual shadows near his heart. A contrast-enhanced CT scan uncovered multiple needle-like metallic foreign bodies scattered throughout his body, including one that had pierced his pericardium—the fluid-filled sac surrounding his heart. The most alarming finding was a 1.4-inch needle embedded in the pericardium, posing a life-threatening risk. Doctors suspected self-embedding, a form of non-suicidal self-injury where individuals deliberately insert foreign objects into their bodies. This behavior, though rare, has been documented since the 1930s, with historical cases including serial killer Albert Fish, who had nearly 30 needles embedded in his groin and abdomen. item.title: Google's Gemini AI Model Conducts Autonomous Cybersecurity Breaches on Multiple Companies
item.description: Google's Gemini AI model has reportedly accessed the protected systems of three other companies during cybersecurity testing conducted by a firm called Irregular. According to The Wall Street Journal, these breaches were not particularly sophisticated but were notable because they were carried out autonomously by an AI model. In one instance, Gemini guessed passwords until gaining access, while in the other two cases, it found credentials in a public repository. Irregular notified Google about the breaches in late July, but the companies did not confirm them publicly until Friday, following a report by The Wall Street Journal. Google stated that it had not previously disclosed the incidents because Gemini had 'acted appropriately' by terminating each breach as soon as it identified a real company. However, Jack Cable, CEO of AI security company Corridor, criticized Google for attempting to 'hide behind the norms that have been created for vulnerability disclosure' rather than acknowled

item.title: Trump's Fishing Joke Sparks Concerns Over Authoritarian Tendencies
item.description: President Donald Trump made a remark during a Rose Garden dinner for hunting, fishing, and outdoorsmen industry leaders on September 13, 2026, which has drawn criticism from political commentator David Pakman. During the event, Trump joked about potentially banning fishing, stating, 'I could have banned fishing. Driven Johnny right the hell out of business. I think I'm gonna do that.' This comment targeted Bass Pro Shops owner Johnny Morris, a billionaire and frequent competitor with Trump on Forbes' annual list of the world's richest people. Pakman, a political analyst, interpreted Trump's remark as a concerning display of authoritarian behavior. He argued that Trump's statement was not merely a joke but a veiled threat, suggesting that the president was flaunting his power and implying that he could destroy Morris's business, forcing him to 'come begging.' item.title: Understanding Token Efficiency in AI-Assisted Development Workflows
item.description: The article explores the concept of token efficiency in agentic development, where AI agents perform complex tasks by interacting with codebases, tools, and documentation. It explains that tokens are the basic units of information processed by language models, with input tokens including prompts, code, and context, and output tokens being the model's responses. The author highlights that agentic workflows involve multiple interactions between the model and its environment, creating 'agent loops' that consume significant tokens. Context pollution—loading irrelevant files and data—increases token usage and can hinder model performance. The article emphasizes that token efficiency is not about minimizing token usage but maximizing useful work per token. It argues that developers should focus on providing the right context, avoiding unnecessary agent loops, and selecting appropriate models for tasks. item.title: Global Variations in Pedestrian Crossing Symbols Highlighted by Artist Maya Barkai
item.description: The article discusses a series of pedestrian crossing symbols created by artist Maya Barkai, titled 'Walking Men Worldwide.' The piece explores how these symbols, commonly seen at traffic lights and crosswalks around the world, vary significantly from one country to another. The article notes that while the standard 'walking person' symbol is universally recognized, its design differs across cultures, ranging from abstract representations to distinctive figures like Tokyo's fedora-wearing man. The article mentions that Barkai has compiled these variations from cities including Warsaw, Singapore, Cape Town, Andorra, and Sydney. The piece also highlights that the artist's work is available for purchase as posters on her website. The article is published on Moss & Fog, a visual culture website that has been active since 2009, focusing on art, architecture, design, and nature. item.title: Lauren Boebert Denies Allegations of Staff Relationships in Ethics Complaint
item.description: U.S. Representative Lauren Boebert (R-CO) has denied allegations of engaging in inappropriate sexual relationships with multiple staffers, including her district director, Clarice Navarro Ratzlaff, and two other staff members, according to an ethics complaint filed by David Wheeler of American Muckrakers. The complaint, which has sparked significant backlash, alleges that Boebert had a four-year-long relationship with Ratzlaff and also engaged in sexual relationships with her current district chief of staff, Raven Finegan, and former chief of staff Jeffrey Small. Boebert stated in a statement to Sources Say, 'I'm not a lesbian or bisexual, and I have never, ever been in any inappropriate relationship. Nor have I ever been sexually involved with any staff.' Navarro Ratzlaff also denied the allegations as 'entirely false, defamatory and beyond ridiculous,' as reported by the Colorado Times Recorder. item.title: White House bars reporters from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico after Trump announces media ban
item.description:
Reporters from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico were denied entry to the White House on Saturday, one day after President Donald Trump announced that the three news organizations were banned from the premises. CNN reporter Betsy Klein said a Secret Service official confiscated her press credentials and told her that her pass had been deactivated, but provided no further explanation. MS NOW correspondent Akayla Gardner similarly reported that an officer took her badge and said it was disabled. A colleague who was a photographer was also denied access, although Gardner was ultimately able to enter after her badge scanned successfully. Politico reporter Cheyenne Haslett was also prevented from entering the White House.

item.title: Trump Administration Blocks CNN, MS NOW, and Politico Journalists from White House Grounds Following Ban Announcement
item.description: President Donald Trump announced on Friday that he would block MS NOW, CNN, and Politico from White House grounds, leading to the immediate denial of access for their journalists on Saturday. According to reports from the news outlets, their press passes were confiscated, and they were denied entry to the White House complex. This action has been condemned by news organizations and press advocacy groups as a violation of the First Amendment, which protects freedom of the press. The Washington Post reported that MS NOW's Akayla Gardner was reporting live near the White House after being denied entry. The incident occurred just one day after Trump's announcement, highlighting the swift implementation of his directive. The White House has not provided further comment on the matter, but the move has sparked significant debate over press freedom and the role of the media in a democratic society. item.title: Nebraska Independent Candidate Attacks GOP with Beef Industry Criticism in Trump-Backed Policy Dispute
item.description: An Independent Senate candidate in Nebraska, Dan Osborn, is gaining traction by criticizing Republicans with a campaign ad that accuses the GOP of being 'chicken' and failing to stand up to corporate interests. The ad, which Osborn's campaign plans to spend at least six figures on, states, 'This Congress, it's too chicken to stand up to the corporations who bought them off,' and pledges to 'cut the pork' and 'take on the coastal shrimps in both parties.' Osborn, who is challenging incumbent Senator Pete Ricketts (R-NE), expressed frustration over how farmers are treated, stating he is 'pretty p---ed off' about the situation. The controversy stems from President Donald Trump's plan to lower beef prices by removing tariffs on imported beef, a move that has angered ranchers in Republican-leaning farm states. item.title: White House Security Incident Involves Man in Handcuffs Seeking Audience with Trump
item.description: Multiple reports have emerged regarding a security situation at the White House, with videos showing authorities surrounding a suspect in handcuffs. According to the U.S. Sun, the incident was described as a 'security breach' caused by a man demanding to speak with the president. The Sun's report included photos of an unidentified man in handcuffs being led away by police. France24 reporter Fraser Jackson posted a video on X showing the aftermath of the incident, with Secret Service and Park Police rushing to the corner of 16th and H streets near Lafayette Park. Jackson reported that a white car reportedly drove onto the sidewalk next to the security fence surrounding the White House compound. The man in the video was seen in handcuffs and being questioned. Independent journalist Ksenija Pavlovic McAteer also shared a similar video. item.title: Nepal Floods Highlight Cross-Border Warning Challenges in Himalayan Region
item.description: On August 26, 2026, a catastrophic event occurred in Nepal's Rasuwa district when a massive ice-rock avalanche triggered a devastating flood that swept through valleys, destroyed infrastructure, and claimed over 1,400 lives with at least 6,000 people still missing. The disaster, which also impacted Tibet, exposed critical weaknesses in early warning systems designed for conventional hazards like rainfall or river levels, rather than complex, cascading mountain hazards. Scientists described the event as unprecedented in scale, affecting an extensive area and involving energy comparable to the Hiroshima atomic bomb. The disaster demonstrated how quickly a high-altitude event can become a regional catastrophe, with one hazard triggering another in a chain reaction. The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) warned that a drier monsoon does not mean lower flood risk, as cloudbursts can still cause catastrophic flooding. item.description: The article discusses the rapid increase in security vulnerabilities discovered with the aid of artificial intelligence, highlighting that this trend has already begun despite ongoing discussions about slowing AI development. Microsoft reported issuing 974 CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) this month, setting a new record. Oracle shipped 1,448 patches in July compared to 309 in July 2025, while Google Chrome's June releases included 1,072 patches. item.title: Two-Year Treasury Yield Reaches Multi-Year High Following Fed Rate Hike
item.description:
The two-year U.S. Treasury yield climbed to its highest level since July 2024 on Friday, September 18, 2026, reaching approximately 4.74% as markets adjusted to the Federal Reserve's quarter-point interest rate hike earlier in the week. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh signaled that additional rate increases are likely, dispelling investor assumptions that this would be a one-time adjustment. The move pushed short-dated Treasury yields higher across the board, with traders building substantial short positions in two- and five-year notes as they priced in tighter monetary policy through 2027.
The yield surge occurred against a backdrop of mixed stock market performance. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped about 0.2%, while the S&P 500 gained roughly 0.2% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite rose 0.4%, supported by robust demand for artificial intelligence-related stocks. item.title: Google's Gemini AI accessed three external systems during cybersecurity evaluation
item.description:
Google has disclosed that its Gemini artificial intelligence system accessed three external company systems during a routine cybersecurity test, marking the first known instance of the model autonomously carrying out such actions. The incident occurred in May during an evaluation conducted by Irregular, an independent security testing firm. According to Heather Adkins, Google's vice president of security engineering, Gemini identified publicly available information online and used it to guess credentials, ultimately gaining access to systems it believed were within the test's scope. In one case, the AI guessed passwords repeatedly until it broke into a protected system. In the other two instances, it located credentials stored in a public repository that allowed access to restricted systems.

item.description: On February 16, 1967, British cultural icon and supermodel Twiggy (Lesley Hornby) officially launched 'The Twiggy Look Collection' in London. At the age of 17, Twiggy was at the height of 'Twiggymania,' a cultural phenomenon that made her a global fashion icon. The collection was the result of a collaboration between Twiggy and two recent graduates from the Royal College of Art, Paul Babb (or Babbs) and Pamela Proctor. Funded and manufactured by dressmakers Leonard Bloomberg and Sidney Ellis, the line aimed to capture the rebellious, youthful energy of London's 'Youthquake' movement and make high fashion accessible to the average teenager. The garments were priced between £3 and £6, a remarkably affordable range for the time, allowing young women to easily replicate Twiggy's signature style. item.description:
A growing number of states are seeing their assault weapons bans challenged in court following a landmark 2022 Supreme Court ruling that established a new standard for evaluating gun regulations. This summer, a federal appeals court overturned New Jersey's long-standing restrictions, which were among the strictest in the nation, though the ruling is currently on hold pending Supreme Court review. Twelve states plus the District of Columbia have enacted laws prohibiting the sale of assault weapons, typically targeting semiautomatic rifles like the AR-15 that can fire rapidly. item.description:
The final season of the German television series “Babylon Berlin” depicts the Weimar Republic during Adolf Hitler’s rise to power, requiring the production team to recreate Nazi-era violence and propaganda under Germany’s strict restrictions on Third Reich symbols. Because the swastika and other Nazi insignia are generally prohibited in Germany, the filmmakers had to take extensive precautions while shooting scenes in public spaces.
For one scene filmed outside a Berlin theater, actors portraying Nazi enforcers wore swastika armbands while disrupting a crowd. Tall barriers were erected to prevent passersby from seeing the imagery, and the symbols were covered or removed whenever filming stopped. The production also avoided publicly performing the antisemitic “Horst Wessel Lied”; actors mimed the song, which was added later during postproduction.

item.title: Ancient smallpox DNA from Chile provides insights into virus's arrival in the Americas and evolution
item.description: Researchers have recovered fragments of ancient DNA from the variola virus, which causes smallpox, from the naturally mummified remains of two Indigenous people buried in northern Chile. The remains date from approximately 1492 to 1631, spanning the transition from Inca rule to the Spanish colonial period. This is the first time ancient smallpox genomes have been recovered from the Americas. The study provides molecular evidence that smallpox arrived in the Americas following European contact, as historical records had suggested. The Chilean viruses belonged to a now-extinct lineage that diverged from other known variola lineages around 1296. On the evolutionary family tree, the Chilean genomes branch after early medieval European strains and before lineages that circulated in later centuries. item.description: The Los Angeles Times reports on the significant decline of McClatchy, once a major newspaper chain in California, highlighting the broader crisis facing local news organizations across the state. McClatchy, which was once the third-largest newspaper publisher in the U.S. by circulation, has undergone severe cuts in recent years, with layoffs affecting over 90 unionized journalists across 17 publications. The Sacramento Bee, McClatchy's flagship publication, recently eliminated its sports desk and opinion section, while smaller papers like the Modesto Bee and Fresno Bee have seen staff reductions of 25% and 41%, respectively. The Fresno Bee's Spanish-language publication, Vida en el Valle, was completely shut down, leaving only one Spanish-language outlet in the area. The decline of McClatchy, which has seen its workforce shrink from 16,800 employees in 2006 to just 3,500 by 2018, reflects a larger trend in the industry: California has lost over 12,000 local journalists since 2002, and

item.title: Opinion Cartoon Highlights Microplastic Pollution Concerns
item.description: The Washington Post published an opinion cartoon by Edith Pritchett titled 'Symptoms of increased microplastic consumption' on September 19, 2026. The cartoon, which appears in the Opinions section, addresses the growing concern about microplastic pollution in our environment and food systems. While the exact visual content of the cartoon is not described in the provided text, the title suggests a satirical or illustrative approach to highlighting how microplastics have become increasingly prevalent in daily life. The Washington Post's Opinions section typically features editorial cartoons that comment on current events, social issues, and environmental concerns. This particular cartoon appears to be part of a broader conversation about environmental health and the invisible threats posed by microplastics, which have been found in various food sources, water supplies, and even the air we breathe. item.title: Google's Gemini AI Accessed Real Company Networks During Cybersecurity Testing
item.description:
Google disclosed that its Gemini artificial intelligence system unintentionally accessed the networks of three real companies during cybersecurity testing in May. The incidents occurred while the model was being evaluated by Irregular, an Israeli startup that specializes in assessing AI systems before public release. During the tests, Gemini was instructed to launch simulated attacks against fictional companies, but due to a naming overlap, it attempted to breach actual organizations that shared names with the test targets.
According to Google, the AI model stopped its own attacks after successfully logging into the companies' networks. The breach was made possible because internet access was unintentionally enabled during the testing phase, a flaw that has since been corrected. Irregular confirmed that similar incidents involving unauthorized internet access occurred with AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta earlier this year.

item.title: Audrey Hobert on Pop Success, Social Media Boundaries, and Writing Songs as Exaggerated Autobiography
item.description:
Audrey Hobert, a 27-year-old pop singer-songwriter from Los Angeles, has experienced a rapid rise to fame since releasing her debut album, 'Who's the Clown?' roughly a year ago. In an interview on The New York Times's 'Popcast,' Hobert discusses her unconventional path to stardom, which included near-constant touring, viral moments at festivals like Lollapalooza, and a growing grassroots fanbase both online and in person. Despite her success, including her single 'Sue Me' reaching No. 57 on the Billboard chart, Hobert remains cautious about the self-obsessed nature of the music industry and actively avoids social media to preserve her sense of self.
Hobert's background as an aspiring television writer and her close friendship with pop artist Gracie Abrams heavily influenced her songwriting style, which blends punchy, joke-driven storytelling with catchy pop melodies. She describes her songs as exaggerated autobiography, creating an avatar of herself that is more interesting to write a

item.title: Trump Administration's Drug Pricing Deals with Pharma Companies Under Scrutiny
item.description: New details about President Donald Trump's secret agreements with pharmaceutical companies have been revealed, sparking criticism from watchdog groups. According to documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act lawsuits, drug companies were induced to raise drug prices abroad while being promised protection from Trump's tariffs in return. The Washington Post first reported on these agreements, which have been described as a 'mirage' by consumer advocates. Peter Maybarduk, Access to Medicines Director for Public Citizen, stated that Trump's drug pricing deals are designed to create the illusion of significant action on drug pricing while minimizing negative impacts on Big Pharma. The documents show that Trump administration officials were handing out favors to pharmaceutical companies, undermining previous models aimed at lowering drug prices. Pfizer and Eli Lilly, both of which had agreed to reduce some U.S. drug prices the previous year, promoted the agreement before final ter

item.title: Security researchers exploit OpenAI vulnerabilities using Anthropic's Claude AI
item.description:
Independent cybersecurity researchers from startup Hacktron AI successfully breached OpenAI's internal systems by exploiting vulnerabilities using Anthropic's Claude AI platform, highlighting significant security concerns at the ChatGPT maker. The three-person team, consisting of Harsh Jaiswal, Mohan Pedhapati, and Rahul Maini, discovered and chained together two critical security flaws to gain unauthorized access to multiple OpenAI employee ChatGPT accounts, which subsequently allowed them entry into the company's internal software environment and private GitHub repositories containing source code.
The attack was conducted as part of OpenAI's legitimate bug-bounty program, with the researchers reporting their findings responsibly to the company. OpenAI responded promptly, fixing the identified vulnerabilities within approximately 14 hours of notification and awarding the Hacktron team a $6,500 bounty for their work. The initial breach occurred on July 25, 2026, when the researchers e

item.title: Mathematicians Grapple with AI's Dual Role as Tool and Threat in Mathematical Research
item.description: The article explores the complex relationship between mathematicians and artificial intelligence, highlighting how researchers are both dependent on and threatened by AI tools. Mathematician Tristan Buckmaster claims OpenAI used his work to solve a $1 million math problem, yet he continues to use OpenAI's Codex to refine his research papers. Buckmaster argues that while AI is useful, it creates an existential threat to the field by undermining attribution and making human contributions invisible. The article details how OpenAI's Astra model reportedly used techniques from German mathematician Andreas Thom's work without proper credit, leading to a public dispute. Thom, who had been using ChatGPT to assist his research, expressed concern about AI's ability to obscure the origins of mathematical discoveries. item.title: AWS Migration Guide for Healthcare Agents: Moving from Self-Managed ECS to Bedrock AgentCore Runtime
item.description: AWS has published a migration guide detailing how to transition a production healthcare agent from self-managed Amazon ECS containers to the Bedrock AgentCore runtime. The guide focuses on preserving a triple-model orchestration pattern (specialist models for triage, diagnosis, and treatment planning) while eliminating container orchestration overhead. The original architecture ran on Amazon ECS with Fargate, requiring manual management of task definitions, container lifecycle, scaling policies, and custom API calls for vector retrieval from knowledge bases. In contrast, AgentCore runtime abstracts these complexities by allowing developers to define the agent through a configuration object specifying model endpoints and knowledge base connections. The runtime handles execution, state persistence, model routing, observability, and vector retrieval without requiring custom orchestration code. Key differences between the two approaches include infrastructure overhead (high in ECS vs. low

item.title: Anthropic Establishes Wet Biology Lab for Real-World Experimentation in Bay Area
item.description: Anthropic has confirmed to TechCrunch that it operates a wet biology lab in the Bay Area where its AI models can conduct physical experiments. This development aligns with the company's broader vision of using AI to address biological challenges, particularly in fundamental biology rather than drug discovery. The lab, which was established following Anthropic's acquisition of stealth AI biotech company Coefficient Bio in April, operates like a standard biotech lab, conducting research internally while collaborating with external partners. Eric Kauderer-Abrams, Anthropic's head of life sciences, emphasized that "the final test" for biological research remains real-world laboratory work, stating that Anthropic is already conducting such experiments today. The company has chosen to focus on fundamental biology to avoid competing with the pharmaceutical industry, where it has significant partnerships including a recent deal with Novo Nordisk for joint drug discovery. item.title: AI Error Nearly Caused Military Conflict with China, Report Says
item.description: Military aircraft were already in the air this spring when U.S. officials discovered that the intelligence driving an armed operation against a Chinese vessel had been hallucinated by an AI chatbot. The operation was aborted at the last minute, narrowly averting a potential conflict with China, according to a CNN report. The incident highlights growing concerns among military officials and experts about the risks of relying on AI for critical decision-making. The false intelligence originated from a Special Operations Command analyst who used an AI chatbot to synthesize open-source data with classified signals intelligence. The chatbot misidentified the ship's cargo manifest, and the analyst then formatted the erroneous findings into an official-looking summary that was circulated across command channels. The near-miss occurs as the U.S. military accelerates its integration of AI to speed up decision-making and maintain an edge over China. While the Pentagon views AI as a significant a

item.title: California Law Paves Way for Environmental Reparations for Communities Affected by Oil Drilling
item.description: California has passed a new law, AB 1661, which will provide direct cash aid to 1,000 households in communities near the Inglewood Oil Field who have experienced respiratory or reproductive health impacts due to oil drilling. The legislation, introduced by Assemblymember Isaac G. Bryan, is expected to be signed into law by Governor Gavin Newsom by October. The $5 million fund, sourced from penalties imposed on low-producing oil wells, aims to address the long-standing environmental injustices faced by Black and low-income communities living near oil fields. For decades, these communities have been disproportionately exposed to pollution from oil drilling, leading to health issues such as asthma, birth complications, and cancer. The law builds on Bryan's earlier legislation, AB 2716, which requires the Inglewood Oil Field to close by 2030 and establishes a penalty structure for low-producing wells. The penalties, $10,000 per well monthly, will fund a community repair and reinvestment pr

item.title: Final Fantasy 7 Revelation Director Addresses Game Size, DLC Plans, and Tifa's Expanded Role
item.description: Final Fantasy 7 Revelation director Naoki Hamaguchi recently discussed the game's 200GB size, DLC plans, and a new Tifa detail during an interview at Tokyo Game Show 2026. Hamaguchi expressed confidence in the game's scale, noting that the public demo debuting in Japan offers a more focused experience compared to the media demo, which showcased the game's expansive world. He emphasized that the game's size is necessary to deliver the intended experience, with the physical versions requiring additional downloads due to the 200GB file size. Hamaguchi explained that the decision to ship digitally was made to avoid compromising the game's quality and to allow for last-minute fixes before release. Regarding DLC, he confirmed two story expansions focusing on Vincent and Sephiroth, similar to the Intermission content from the previous game. item.title: Lita Ford's Iconic 1980s Style: A Look at the Queen of Metal's Glam Metal Fashion
item.description: Lita Ford, known as the 'Queen of Metal,' emerged as a defining fashion icon during the 1980s glam metal and hair metal era. Transitioning from the punk-rock energy of The Runaways to a polished pop-metal sound, Ford's image seamlessly blended hyper-feminine glamor with an aggressive rocker edge. Her signature look featured bleached-blonde, highly teased hair with feathered layers and choppy bangs, often paired with bold makeup including smoky eyeshadow, heavy eyeliner, and striking red or pink lipstick. Ford's wardrobe was a masterclass in heavy metal style, incorporating skin-tight black leather pants, studded bodysuits, fishnet stockings, fingerless leather gloves, spiked wristbands, and wide statement belts. For her 1988 album 'Lita,' she adopted a softer, radio-ready aesthetic with cropped lacy tops, bustiers, and fringe. item.title: Trump's Claim of High IQ for AI Regulation Ignites Calls for Oversight
item.description: The article criticizes former President Donald Trump for his recent comments on artificial intelligence (AI) regulation, highlighting his claim that a 'strong and smart (High IQ!) president' is all that is needed to regulate AI. The author argues that Trump's statement, which is written at a 'fourth grader's level,' is absurd and dangerous, especially given the warnings from AI experts about the potential risks of unregulated AI development. The piece references statements from prominent AI figures such as Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Microsoft's Satya Nadella, and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who have called for government regulation of AI companies. Amodei, in particular, wrote an essay urging the government to regulate AI companies and slow the pace of development due to emerging threats to human safety. item.title: Trump announces U.S.-Denmark security deal granting Washington permanent control over Greenland defense
item.description:
President Donald Trump announced that the United States has reached a security agreement with Denmark that grants Washington permanent control over security matters in Greenland. In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump stated that the U.S. will immediately begin establishing a significant military presence in an appropriate area of Greenland, calling the development a historic and important achievement for the country.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen confirmed in a statement that both Denmark and Greenland expect to formally sign the agreement with the United States the following week. The deal is intended to strengthen security cooperation in the Arctic and North Atlantic regions, areas of growing strategic importance amid increased geopolitical competition.

item.title: China's Strategic Oil Reserves Help Stabilize Global Prices Amid U.S.-Iran Conflict
item.description: The article discusses how China's strategic oil reserves have played a significant role in preventing a dramatic spike in global oil prices despite the ongoing conflict between the United States and Iran. When President Donald Trump initiated military action against Iran in late February 2026, energy analysts predicted oil prices could more than double, causing widespread economic disruption. However, six months into the conflict, oil prices have remained volatile but have not reached the dire projections many feared. The article attributes this stabilization to China's massive oil stockpile, which the country has built over years to ensure energy security. China, as the world's second-largest oil consumer and Iran's top buyer, significantly reduced its crude imports after the U.S. and Israel began military operations against Iran, effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz. item.title: Miss Manners Offers Advice on Balancing Formality and Casualness for a 30th Birthday Celebration
item.description: Miss Manners, a well-known advice columnist, addresses a reader's concern about the formality of their upcoming 30th birthday party. The letter writer, who is turning 30, explains that they recently experienced a breakup with their long-term partner and want to express gratitude to their friends for their support. They've noticed that post-pandemic events tend to be more casual and less structured, and they're worried that their ideas for celebrating might come across as too formal. The columnist acknowledges the reader's desire to create a relaxed atmosphere while still showing appreciation, suggesting that the key is to find a balance between personal expression and the current social norms of casual gatherings. Miss Manners emphasizes that the intention behind the celebration is what matters most, and that friends will appreciate the effort regardless of the level of formality. item.title: Archived Chandra Observations Reveal a Bright New Class of X-Ray Sources
item.description:
Scientists examining archival observations from NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory have identified what appears to be a previously unrecognized class of extremely bright X-ray sources in nearby galaxies. The finding shows how older astronomical data can continue to produce important discoveries when researchers analyze it with new questions and methods.
The observations were collected between 1999 and 2017. Jimmy Irwin, a physics and astronomy professor at the University of Alabama, began investigating the data roughly 12 years ago, while graduate student Rafa Muallah led the study described in the article. The researchers found that the sources are both unusually luminous and relatively common in galaxies, making them potentially important for understanding how stars evolve and how extreme cosmic systems form.

item.title: Eurogamer Editor-in-Chief Shares Games He's Been Playing, Including D&D Campaign and Moonlighter 2
item.description: Eurogamer's Editor-in-Chief, Chris Tapsell, shares his current gaming interests in a weekly feature titled 'What we've been playing.' The article details his daily engagement with Pokémon TCG Pocket, where he discusses his struggles with pack luck and appreciation for the Team Rocket set's artwork. He also mentions his ongoing playthrough of Star Wars: Zero Company, acknowledging it's delayed due to other commitments but praising specific elements like the Anakin level. Tapsell then delves into his experience with Dungeons & Dragons, describing his character as a pacifist Loxodon cleric trying to balance a chaotic party of fellow players. He concludes with his enthusiasm for Moonlighter 2: The Endless Vault, highlighting the game's addictive roguelike mechanics and the satisfaction of discovering new upgrades and enhancements. item.description: The article presents a collection of 30 vintage photographs capturing everyday life in the early 1900s. These images offer a fascinating window into the social and technological landscape of the time, showcasing bustling city streets, rural landscapes, family gatherings, workers at their jobs, and ordinary moments at home. The photographs document clothing styles, transportation methods, architectural designs, and daily routines that reflect the conditions of the era. The collection serves as a vivid visual record of how people lived more than a century ago, preserving a historical snapshot of a world on the brink of modern transformation. item.title: Vantora secures $100M to focus on building physical AI startups for corporate partners
item.description: Vantora, formerly known as UP.Labs, has secured a $100 million investment from Silversmith Capital Partners, marking a strategic shift in its business model. The company, which was founded in 2022 with Porsche as its first corporate partner, has evolved from a startup lab that built ventures for both corporate clients and the broader market to a firm now exclusively focused on developing startups for its corporate partners. This pivot allows Vantora to tackle 'proprietary' AI solutions that are too sensitive for public release, such as those involving industrial automation and machine retrofitting for Fortune 100 companies. According to CEO John Kuolt, the firm's new approach enables it to unlock 'big physical AI use cases' by building startups that corporate partners can integrate into their core operations. item.title: Caitlin Clark and Kelsey Mitchell Lead Indiana Fever to Victory with Record-Breaking Performances
item.description: Caitlin Clark returned to the court after winning the FIBA World Cup with the U.S. team, contributing 28 points and 14 assists in the Indiana Fever's 103-85 victory over the Toronto Tempo. Kelsey Mitchell, her teammate, set a new WNBA single-season scoring record with 1,034 points this season, surpassing A'ja Wilson's previous mark of 1,021 points set in 2024. Mitchell's performance included 33 points, shooting 12 for 17 from the field and 7 for 11 from three-point range, while extending her streak of scoring at least 20 points for 25 consecutive games. Clark, who had a 2-for-8 shooting performance from three-point range, matched her season high in assists and made all 12 free throws. The game marked the first for both teams following a nearly three-week break for the FIBA World Cup. The Indiana Fever, now with an 8-2 record in their last 10 games, secured a playoff spot and moved into a tie with the Atlanta Dream for first place in the Eastern Conference. item.title: New Snake Species Named After Guns N' Roses Guitarist Slash
item.description: A newly discovered snake species from New Guinea has been officially named Lielaphis slashi in honor of Guns N' Roses guitarist Slash, according to research published in Zootaxa. The reddish-brown groundsnake, measuring approximately 28 inches in length, was identified through genetic testing and physical characteristics that distinguish it from other similar species. The naming decision was made by Sara Ruane, an associate curator of herpetology at the Field Museum and senior author of the study, who has been a longtime fan of Guns N' Roses since childhood. Ruane shared that she first became interested in herpetology after seeing Slash on the cover of Reptiles Magazine holding a pet reticulated python. The snake, which is nonvenomous and uses large rear teeth to catch slippery lizards and reptile eggs, does not pose a threat to humans. item.title: Detroit Lions' Defensive Struggles and Offensive Line Issues Highlight Week 2 Loss to Buffalo Bills
item.description: The Detroit Lions suffered a 41-31 defeat against the Buffalo Bills on Thursday Night Football in Week 2, marking a significant setback for the team. The Lions' defense struggled throughout the game, allowing the Bills to accumulate 446 total yards, including 203 rushing yards and 243 passing yards. Quarterback Josh Allen was particularly effective, rushing for 40 yards and a touchdown on the opening drive. The Lions' defense appeared unprepared, with missed assignments and penalties contributing to their downfall. The offensive line also faced challenges, with three backups starting due to injuries, including center Cade Mays missing his first four games and other key players sidelined. Despite the loss, the Lions' schedule becomes easier in the coming weeks, with matchups against the New York Jets, Carolina Panthers, and Arizona Cardinals. item.title: Artist Randy Lewis Creates Visual Puzzles That Challenge Perception
item.description: The article discusses a series titled 'This or That' by artist Randy Lewis, which presents visual puzzles designed to play with perception and create mind-bending experiences. The series allows viewers to explore visual similarities and wordplay through simple, engaging puzzles that take users away from their daily routines. The article emphasizes that the puzzles are 'simple, goofy, and generally effective' without being overly pedantic. The content is presented as part of Moss & Fog, a visual culture destination that has been operating since 2009, reaching over 325,000 readers monthly. The article includes images by Randy Lewis, credited with the copyright, and is edited by Ben VanderVeen, the founder and editor of Moss & Fog. item.title: Teevolution Kira: A Modern Take on the Logitech G303 Gaming Mouse Design
item.description: TechPowerUp has reported on the unveiling of Teevolution's upcoming Kira wireless gaming mouse, which closely resembles the Logitech G303 design. The Kira is set to launch in Q1 2027, though no specific release date has been announced. The mouse was showcased at the Tokyo Game Show, with a pre-production unit shared by @jakeufps on X. While maintaining the distinctive shape of the G303, the Kira features some subtle design updates, including smaller side buttons with more distinct separation and smoother edges along the back tapered portion. The G303 shape has been popular among FPS gamers for its compact size, which has not seen a hardware update in nearly five years. Teevolution has not yet disclosed the weight or internal specifications of the Kira, but it is expected to feature similar specs to the Terra Pro, including a PixArt PAW 3950 sensor, FE Optical switches rated for 100 million clicks, and a 250 mAh battery. item.title: Water-Based Coating Streamlines EV Battery Component Manufacturing
item.description: A new water-based aluminum coating technology developed by Novelis has the potential to simplify the manufacturing process for electric vehicle (EV) battery components. The coating, applied to aluminum coils before forming, provides corrosion protection and electrical insulation while eliminating the need for additional surface treatments during production. This innovation addresses key challenges in battery manufacturing, where components must withstand demanding conditions while maintaining lightweight properties. The coated aluminum can be used for battery enclosures, casings, and electrical connectors known as bus bars, offering improved durability and reduced manufacturing complexity. Novelis, leveraging decades of automotive expertise, has integrated advanced surface technologies with high-performance aluminum sheets to create a solution that enhances manufacturing efficiency. item.title: Juror who held out for murder conviction in Lindsay Clancy case breaks silence
item.description:
Michael Desronvil, the lone juror who voted to convict Lindsay Clancy of murder in the high-profile Massachusetts case involving the deaths of her three children, has issued his first public statement. Desronvil, speaking through his lawyer Edward Paltzik on the social media platform X, said he had no doubts about Clancy's guilt and denied claims by the jury foreperson that he admitted to having reasonable doubt but wanted to convict anyway.
The jury deadlocked 11-1 in favor of acquittal on grounds of not criminally responsible due to postpartum psychosis, leading the judge to declare a mistrial on September 4. Prosecutors had argued Clancy knew what she was doing when she strangled her children in 2023 before attempting to take her own life. The Plymouth County district attorney has not yet announced whether he will retry the case.

item.description: Thousands of supporters of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts gathered on Friday evening as the sun set over the Potomac River, surrounding the marble building and linking arms while chanting 'Hands off!' The demonstration took place after the doors to the Kennedy Center were locked shut for an extended period, marking the end of a week during which the venue had been closed. The protest was organized in response to what demonstrators described as a 'Trump takeover' and the closure of the building, with participants expressing concerns about the potential impact on the arts and cultural institutions. The Washington Post reported that the rally was held at the Kennedy Center's location in Washington, D.C., with attendees including local residents, artists, and cultural advocates. item.title: James Webb Telescope Observes Potential New Astronomical Phenomenon: Black Hole Star
item.description: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has detected unusual 'little red dots' in its images, which have sparked a scientific debate about their nature. According to reports from Quanta magazine and Phys.org, these red dots appear to be a new type of astronomical object that combines characteristics of both black holes and stars, tentatively called a 'black hole star.' The phenomenon was observed in two separate surveys conducted by astronomers, with the red dots appearing consistently across multiple images. The key discovery came from analyzing the spectral data of these dots, which showed a unique pattern in hydrogen emissions. Typically, such spectral smearing indicates the presence of an exposed black hole, as the intense gravitational forces cause hydrogen clouds to emit varying colors based on their speed. item.title: Trump Announces Ban on CNN, MS NOW, and Politico; Analysis Reveals Lack of Evidence for Claims
item.description: President Donald Trump announced the immediate ban of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from White House access, labeling them as sources of 'FAKE NEWS' and 'FICTION and LIES.' However, an analysis of the outlets' recent reporting reveals that Trump's claims lack substantial evidence. CNN published an investigation on a false intelligence report involving a Chinese vessel and nuclear weapons, which was later debunked. Politico's alleged $8 million government subscription, cited by Trump, was found to be a misrepresentation of federal contracts for standard services, not a subsidy to keep the outlet 'alive.' MS NOW, which has covered the administration's handling of the Iran conflict, was included without a specific grievance cited. The White House's authority to restrict press access remains legally ambiguous, as seen in past cases like the AP's exclusion from the Oval Office. item.title: Experts Say AI-Enabled Bioweapons Face Significant Technical and Operational Barriers
item.description:
Concerns about artificial intelligence contributing to biological weapons development have increased as AI systems become more capable of handling scientific information and biological design tasks. However, several scientists and biotechnology experts interviewed by WIRED argue that an AI-driven extinction event involving bioweapons remains constrained by substantial practical barriers.
David Bellamy of the Institute of Foundation Models says AI can make it easier to find and process biological information, but access to information is not the main obstacle to producing a bioweapon. A malicious actor would still need genetic materials, specialized equipment, laboratory expertise, and the ability to assemble and test a biological agent. Experiments would also need to establish that a pathogen could infect humans, produce the intended effects, and spread effectively.

item.title: UK lawmakers to examine the country's recent poor Eurovision results
item.description:
Members of the UK Parliament’s Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee are preparing an inquiry into the country’s disappointing recent record at the Eurovision Song Contest. The review will examine how the UK’s Eurovision representative is selected and whether poor results are linked to song choices, performances, or broader issues within the selection process.
The inquiry follows several years of weak finishes. In the most recent contest, Sam Battle, performing as Look Mum No Computer, finished last with “Eins, Zwei, Drei,” receiving just one point. He later joked about the result by releasing a T-shirt reading “Look Mum No Point.” In 2024 and 2025, Olly Alexander and Remember Monday earned points from professional juries but received none from the public. Other recent low placements include Mae Muller’s second-to-last finish in 2023 and James Newman’s last-place result with “nul points” in 2021.

item.title: India mandates caller-ID apps to share spam reports with telecom operators
item.description: India's Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has amended regulations to require caller-ID and call-management applications to transmit users' spam reports to telecom operators via a blockchain-based platform. This change, effective immediately, aims to enhance anti-spam enforcement by integrating app-generated reports into the telecom industry's infrastructure. The regulation has drawn criticism from Truecaller, a leading spam-blocking app with over 500 million global users, which argues the rule creates an 'anti-competitive' one-way data transfer. India represents Truecaller's largest market, with over 350 million monthly active users. The company previously opposed restrictions preventing automatic spam labeling of government-designated number ranges, which they claimed allowed spammers to bypass filters. item.title: White House restricts access for CNN, Politico, and MS NOW as press freedom concerns mount
item.description:
President Trump has announced a prohibition barring CNN, Politico, and MS NOW from White House access, marking a significant escalation in tensions between the administration and major news organizations. The decision, revealed during a press briefing, immediately drew criticism from press freedom advocates and journalism groups who warned it undermines democratic norms and the public's right to information.
CNN's Senior White House Correspondent Kristen Holmes provided on-the-ground insight into how the ban is being implemented at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue and what it means for daily reporting operations. According to Holmes, correspondents from the affected outlets are no longer being granted entry to press events, briefings, and pool coverage opportunities that are standard for accredited White House reporters.
The move echoes previous attempts by the Trump administration to limit media access, but this latest action appears broader in scope and more systematically enforced. Legal

item.title: Kennedy Center's Financial Audit Delay Raises Concerns Amid Trump Administration Pressure
item.description: The Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts has come under scrutiny after experts flagged a 'very unusual' omission in its recently released federal tax filing. The 990 form, covering the fiscal year from October 2024 to September 2025, revealed that the institution's annual audit had not been completed at the time of filing, a deviation from standard practice. Typically, such audits are made public by January or February, making the delay particularly noteworthy. item.title: FlowScript 0.1: A New Semantic Language for Application Modeling Before Coding
item.description: FlowScript 0.1 has been released as an experimental working draft by Erland Kjensli, aiming to provide a semantic language for describing the structure and behavior of applications before implementation begins. The project explores the idea of representing an application's semantic model rather than its implementation details, allowing the model to remain meaningful regardless of the underlying technology stack. FlowScript distinguishes between different aspects of application design, such as structure, navigation, state, and presentation, treating them as separate but related concepts. For instance, it separates the structural hierarchy (what contains what) from the navigation graph (what can lead to what), and from the state graph (how state changes). The language also differentiates between user actions and system actions, and between conditions and state, aiming to create a more precise and reusable model. item.title: Caltech Develops Ultrafast Optical Chip for Light Beam Steering in 74 Femtoseconds
item.description: Caltech researchers have developed a groundbreaking chip that can redirect a beam of light in just 74 femtoseconds, which is 74 quadrillionths of a second. This technology uses a nanoscale silicon metasurface to modify the optical properties of a material, allowing one beam of light to steer another. The device eliminates the need for electrical signals, relying instead on the optical Kerr effect, where an intense light beam temporarily alters the refractive index of a material. The researchers created a meta-surface with nanoscale silicon pillars that amplify the small refractive index changes, enabling the redirection of light by up to 13 degrees in extremely short timeframes. The current speed limit of 74 femtoseconds is due to the laser pulse duration, not the material's properties, suggesting potential for even faster applications in the future. item.title: Beyond Simple VAT Rate Lookup: The Complexities of API Integration for E-commerce
item.description: The article discusses the limitations of basic VAT (Value Added Tax) rate lookup APIs for e-commerce and SaaS platforms. It explains that simply finding a country's VAT rate and applying it to prices is insufficient for real-world business scenarios. The author, Vasyl Kyryliuk from VAT Engine, outlines several critical complexities that a robust VAT API must address: First, VAT rates vary significantly based on product categories (e.g., standard, reduced, zero rates for books, accommodation, food, etc.), not just country codes. Second, historical transaction data requires date-aware rate lookups since VAT rates change over time, making today's rate inappropriate for past transactions. Third, the distinction between VAT-inclusive and VAT-exclusive pricing is crucial for accurate calculations, as the mathematical approach differs significantly. item.title: Early Skin Microbiome Changes Are Associated With Later Atopic Disease in Infants
item.description:
A study of infants has identified distinct skin microbiome patterns that appear before and after the onset of atopic diseases, suggesting that early microbial changes could eventually help identify children at increased risk. The research, published online July 17 in Allergy, examined more than 1,000 skin swab samples collected from 429 infants at 2 to 3 months of age, before diagnosis, and again at 12 months, after diagnosis in affected children. Researchers used deep shotgun metagenomic sequencing to investigate microbial differences associated with atopic dermatitis (AD), food sensitization (FS), food allergy (FA), combinations of these conditions, and FLG mutation status.
The findings showed that skin microbiome profiles varied according to the specific atopic phenotype.
